title: How do we keep the database from becoming the bottleneck?
summary: Fix slow queries first, then cache what is read often and send other reads to replicas. Writes still go to one main database.

lesson.problem: Adding app servers was easy, but they all lean on the same database, which is now the slow part. Looking closer, the team finds that menus are viewed about a hundred times for every order placed, and the same menus are read over and over.
why: Before buying anything, they look at the slowest queries. Two are missing an index. Adding them halves the database load in an afternoon, for free.
Next, a cache. Menus change a few times a day, so the app keeps them in Redis for five minutes and only asks the database when the copy has expired. Most menu reads never reach the database again.

Order history and the restaurants' sales reports move to a read replica: a copy of the database that only answers reads. All writes, like new orders and payments, still go to the main database, so there is one source of truth.

The catch is that copies can be slightly behind. A menu that is a minute old is fine. An order that "disappears" right after you placed it is not, so the order confirmation page reads from the main database.
takeaways: Measure first: indexes and better queries are the cheapest speed-up.
Cache data that is read often and changes rarely.
Read replicas spread reads; writes still go to one primary.
Decide where slightly old data is acceptable and where it isn't.
